title: Literary Criticism
overview: Is unit mein Plato se lekar Russian Formalism tak Western criticism aur Bharata ki Rasa se Kshemendra ke Auchitya tak Indian poetics aate hain. NET mein zyada sawaal famous quotes (kisne kaha), works ke saal, terms ke coiner, match-the-following aur chronology par aate hain.

topics.title: Plato (c. 428-348 BCE): Poetry as Imitation
points: Key works for criticism: Ion, Republic (Books II, III and X), Phaedrus, Symposium; all written as dialogues with Socrates as speaker.
Mimesis: art imitates the world of appearances, which itself copies the world of Ideas/Forms, so art is 'thrice removed from the truth' (Republic X) [satya se teen guna door].
Bed/couch analogy (Republic X): God makes the Idea of bed, the carpenter makes a bed, the painter only paints its appearance.
Republic Book X speaks of 'the ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry' and banishes imitative poets from the ideal state; only hymns to gods and praises of good men allowed.
Moral charge: poetry 'feeds and waters the passions' instead of drying them up, and shows gods and heroes behaving badly (Books II-III).
Book III distinguishes diegesis (simple narration in the poet's own voice) from mimesis (imitation through characters' speech); dithyramb = pure narration, drama = pure imitation, epic = mixed.

Ion: the rhapsode Ion recites Homer; poetry comes from divine inspiration/madness, not art or knowledge; the magnet and iron-rings image shows inspiration passing from Muse to poet to rhapsode to audience.
Phaedrus calls poetic madness a gift of the Muses; Plato himself is called a poet-philosopher who attacked poetry poetically.
Plato's attack is answered by Aristotle (Poetics) and, in English, by Sidney's Apology for Poetry.

topics.title: Aristotle (384-322 BCE): Poetics
points: Poetics (c. 335 BCE), 26 chapters, survives incomplete; the section on comedy is lost. Aristotle was Plato's pupil and tutor of Alexander.

Answers Plato: imitation is natural to man and a source of learning and pleasure; poetry is 'more philosophical and a higher thing than history' because it expresses the universal, history the particular (Ch. 9).

Definition of tragedy (Ch. 6): 'an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude ... through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.'
Six parts of tragedy in order of importance: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Thought (dianoia), Diction (lexis), Song (melos), Spectacle (opsis).
'Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy'; a tragedy is possible without character but not without action.
Plot must have a beginning, middle and end; complex plot contains peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition); third element is pathos (scene of suffering).
The ideal tragic hero is neither wholly good nor wholly bad, of high fortune, who falls through hamartia (error of judgement), e.g. Oedipus; Sophocles' Oedipus Rex is his model tragedy.

Aristotle insists only on unity of action; he notes tragedy tries to keep within 'a single revolution of the sun'; unity of place was added by Castelvetro (1570), making the 'three unities' of neoclassicism.
Comedy imitates men 'worse than the average'; tragedy men better than average; epic differs from tragedy in length and narrative form; tragedy is judged superior to epic (Ch. 26).
Other works: Rhetoric, Politics (catharsis also discussed there), Nicomachean Ethics.

topics.title: Horace (65-8 BCE) and Longinus (1st century CE)
points: Horace's Ars Poetica (also Epistula ad Pisones), verse letter c. 19-18 BCE, addressed to the Piso family; Roman, Latin.
Aim of poetry: to teach and to delight (prodesse et delectare); 'he wins every vote who mixes the useful with the sweet' (utile dulci).

Horatian rules: decorum (fitness of style to character and subject), begin in medias res, five acts, no more than three speaking actors, avoid deus ex machina, no violent deeds like Medea killing her children on stage.

Famous Horatian phrases: 'purple patches' (purpureus pannus), 'ut pictura poesis' (as is painting so is poetry), 'Even good Homer nods', 'the mountains will labour and a ridiculous mouse will be born', keep a work 'nine years' before publishing.
Longinus, Peri Hupsous (On the Sublime), Greek treatise of the 1st century CE, addressed to Postumius Terentianus; author's identity uncertain (Pseudo-Longinus).
Sublimity aims not at persuasion but at transport (ekstasis); 'Sublimity is the echo of a great soul.'

Five sources of the sublime: (1) grandeur of thought, (2) strong and inspired emotion - both innate; (3) proper use of figures, (4) noble diction, (5) dignified and elevated composition (word arrangement) - both acquired by art.
Longinus quotes Sappho's ode ('Phainetai moi') and Genesis 'Let there be light'; compares the Iliad to the midday sun and the Odyssey to the setting sun (Homer in old age).
Boileau's French translation (1674) spread the idea; Burke's Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful (1757) developed it; Longinus is seen as the first romantic critic.

topics.title: Bharata and the Rasa Theory
points: Bharata Muni's Natyashastra (c. 200 BCE-200 CE), 36 chapters (37 in some recensions), called the 'fifth Veda' (Natyaveda); earliest Indian treatise on drama, dance and music.

Rasa Sutra: 'vibhavanubhava-vyabhichari-samyogad rasa-nishpattih' - rasa arises from the union of vibhava (determinants), anubhava (consequents) and vyabhicharibhava (transitory states) [rasa = kavya ka aanand/swad].
Vibhava has two kinds: alambana (the person/object on whom emotion rests) and uddipana (exciting circumstances like moonlight, garden).
Bharata names 8 rasas with 8 sthayibhavas: Shringara-rati, Hasya-hasa, Karuna-shoka, Raudra-krodha, Vira-utsaha, Bhayanaka-bhaya, Bibhatsa-jugupsa, Adbhuta-vismaya.
Ninth rasa, Shanta (sthayibhava nirveda/shama), was accepted later and firmly defended by Abhinavagupta; Vatsalya and Bhakti rasa were added still later (Bhakti by Rupa Goswami).
Bharata lists 33 vyabhicharibhavas (sancharibhavas) and 8 sattvikabhavas (stambha, sveda, romancha, etc.).

Four interpreters of the rasa sutra: Bhatta Lollata - utpattivada (rasa produced in the character); Shri Shankuka - anumitivada (rasa inferred); Bhatta Nayaka - bhuktivada (rasa enjoyed through sadharanikarana); Abhinavagupta - abhivyaktivada (rasa manifested in the spectator).
Abhinavagupta's commentary on the Natyashastra is the Abhinavabharati; the ideal reader is the sahridaya (one of similar heart).
Vishwanatha's Sahityadarpana (14th century) defines poetry as 'vakyam rasatmakam kavyam' (a sentence whose soul is rasa).
Natyashastra also gives four abhinayas (angika, vachika, aharya, sattvika) and four vrittis (kaishiki, sattvati, arabhati, bharati).

topics.title: Dhvani: Anandavardhana and Abhinavagupta
points: Anandavardhana (9th century, Kashmir, court of Avantivarman) wrote the Dhvanyaloka; key claim 'kavyasyatma dhvanih' - suggestion is the soul of poetry.
Three powers (shaktis) of words: abhidha (denotation, literal meaning), lakshana (indication, secondary meaning), vyanjana (suggestion); dhvani works through vyanjana.
Three kinds of dhvani: vastu dhvani (suggestion of a fact/idea), alankara dhvani (suggestion of a figure), rasa dhvani (suggestion of emotion) - rasa dhvani is the highest.
Three grades of poetry: dhvani kavya (uttama, best - suggested sense dominates), gunibhuta vyangya (madhyama - suggested sense subordinate), chitra kavya (adhama - only verbal/figurative ornament).
Anandavardhana united the rasa and dhvani ideas: rasa can never be stated directly, it can only be suggested.
Abhinavagupta (c. 950-1016) wrote Lochana (Dhvanyalokalochana), the commentary on Dhvanyaloka, and Abhinavabharati on the Natyashastra.
Opponent Mahimabhatta (Vyaktiviveka, 11th century) argued dhvani is only inference (anumana); Kuntaka tried to include it in vakrokti.
Mammata's Kavyaprakasha (11th century) firmly established the dhvani school; Jagannatha's Rasagangadhara (17th century) is the last major work.
Dhvani is often compared with Empson's ambiguity and with the idea of suggestion/implicature in Western criticism.

topics.title: Alankara, Riti, Vakrokti and Auchitya Schools
points: Six schools (sampradayas) of Indian poetics: Rasa, Alankara, Riti, Dhvani, Vakrokti, Auchitya.

Alankara school: Bhamaha (Kavyalankara, c. 6th-7th century) - earliest extant alankara text; defines poetry 'shabdarthau sahitau kavyam' (word and meaning together); considers vakrokti the basis of all figures.
Dandin (Kavyadarsha, 7th century) - alankara as 'kavya-shobha-karan dharma' (elements that beautify poetry); also discusses two margas, Vaidarbha and Gauda; Udbhata and Rudrata are later alankarikas.
Alankaras divide into shabdalankara (sound figures: anuprasa, yamaka, shlesha) and arthalankara (sense figures: upama, rupaka, utpreksha).

Riti school: Vamana (Kavyalankarasutravritti, 8th century, court of Jayapida of Kashmir) - 'ritir atma kavyasya' (style is the soul of poetry); riti = 'vishishta padarachana' (special arrangement of words).
Vamana's three ritis: Vaidarbhi (best, has all ten gunas), Gaudi (ojas and kanti, heavy compounds), Panchali (madhurya and saukumarya); Rudrata added Lati.
Vakrokti school: Kuntaka (Vakroktijivita, c. 10th-11th century) - 'vakroktih kavyajivitam' (striking/oblique expression is the life of poetry).

Kuntaka's six levels of vakrata: varna-vinyasa (phoneme), pada-purvardha (word base), pada-parardha (suffix), vakya (sentence), prakarana (episode), prabandha (whole composition); often compared to Russian Formalist defamiliarization.

Auchitya school: Kshemendra (Auchitya-vichara-charcha, 11th century, Kashmir) - 'auchityam rasasiddhasya sthiram kavyasya jivitam' (propriety is the abiding life of poetry full of rasa); comparable to Horace's decorum.
Rough chronology: Bharata - Bhamaha - Dandin - Vamana - Anandavardhana - Abhinavagupta - Kuntaka - Kshemendra - Mammata - Vishwanatha - Jagannatha.

topics.title: Sir Philip Sidney: An Apology for Poetry
points: Written c. 1579-80, published posthumously 1595 in two editions: An Apology for Poetry (Olney) and The Defence of Poesy (Ponsonby).
Occasioned by Stephen Gosson's puritan attack The School of Abuse (1579), which Gosson dedicated to Sidney.
Poet as 'maker' (from Greek poiein) and vates (prophet); the poet is not tied to nature but creates 'another nature'.
'Nature never set forth the earth in so rich tapestry as divers poets have done ... Her world is brazen, the poets only deliver a golden.'
Poetry is 'an art of imitation ... a speaking picture, with this end, to teach and delight' (Horatian echo).
The poet is the 'monarch' of all sciences, superior to the philosopher (precept only) and the historian (example only), since he joins precept and example.
Answer to the charge of lying: 'the poet, he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth.'
Criticises contemporary English drama for breaking the unities and for 'mongrel tragi-comedy'; praises Gorboduc (1561) for its style but faults it on unity of time and place.
Sidney's other works: Astrophel and Stella (sonnet sequence), Arcadia (prose romance); he is the first major English critic of the Renaissance.

topics.title: John Dryden: Father of English Criticism
points: Dr Johnson called Dryden 'the father of English criticism'.
An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668), a dialogue set on a barge on the Thames on 3 June 1665 during the naval battle between the English and the Dutch.

Four speakers: Crites (Sir Robert Howard) defends the Ancients; Eugenius (Lord Buckhurst, Charles Sackville) defends the Moderns; Lisideius (Sir Charles Sedley) praises French drama; Neander (Dryden himself) defends English drama and rhyme.

Lisideius's definition of a play: 'a just and lively image of human nature, representing its passions and humours, and the changes of fortune to which it is subject, for the delight and instruction of mankind.'
On Shakespeare: 'the man who of all modern, and perhaps ancient poets, had the largest and most comprehensive soul'; on Jonson: 'I admire him, but I love Shakespeare.'
Neander examines Jonson's The Silent Woman (Epicoene) as a model of the regular play; defends English tragicomedy and subplots.
Preface to the Fables, Ancient and Modern (1700): calls Chaucer 'the father of English poetry' and says of The Canterbury Tales 'here is God's plenty.'
Other critical prose: Of Heroic Plays (1672), Preface to All for Love (1678), A Discourse Concerning the Original and Progress of Satire (1693) - where he says Donne 'affects the metaphysics'.

topics.title: Alexander Pope and Samuel Johnson
points: Pope's An Essay on Criticism (1711), in heroic couplets, three parts; written when Pope was about 21; neoclassical creed of following Nature and the Ancients.

Pope quotes: 'First follow Nature'; 'A little learning is a dangerous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring'; 'To err is human, to forgive divine'; 'For fools rush in where angels fear to tread.'

'True wit is Nature to advantage dressed, / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed'; 'The sound must seem an echo to the sense'; 'Those rules of old discovered, not devised, / Are Nature still, but Nature methodized.'
Pope also wrote the Preface to his edition of Shakespeare (1725) and Peri Bathous, or the Art of Sinking in Poetry (1728), a parody of Longinus.

Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare (1765): 'Shakespeare is above all writers, at least above all modern writers, the poet of nature; the poet that holds up to his readers a faithful mirror of manners and of life.'
Johnson: Shakespeare's characters are 'commonly a species', not individuals; he defends the mingling of tragic and comic and rejects the unities of time and place, keeping only unity of action.
Johnson's faults list: Shakespeare 'sacrifices virtue to convenience'; 'A quibble is to Shakespeare what luminous vapours are to the traveller ... the fatal Cleopatra for which he lost the world.'

Lives of the Poets (1779-81): in the Life of Cowley Johnson describes the metaphysical poets: 'the most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together'; he popularised the label 'metaphysical poets'.
Rasselas (1759), Imlac: 'The business of a poet is to examine, not the individual, but the species ... he does not number the streaks of the tulip.' Johnson's Dictionary appeared in 1755.

topics.title: William Wordsworth and S. T. Coleridge
points: Lyrical Ballads (1798) by Wordsworth and Coleridge marks the start of English Romanticism; the famous Preface was added in the 1800 edition and enlarged in 1802.
Wordsworth: 'all good poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.'

Aim: to choose 'incidents and situations from common life' and describe them 'in a selection of language really used by men', throwing over them 'a certain colouring of imagination'; rustic life preferred.
Poet is 'a man speaking to men'; poetry is 'the breath and finer spirit of all knowledge'; he attacks 18th-century 'poetic diction', citing Gray's Sonnet on the Death of Richard West.
Wordsworth says there is no essential difference between the language of prose and metrical composition.

Coleridge's Biographia Literaria (1817): Chapter XIII distinguishes primary imagination, secondary imagination and fancy; Chapter XIV gives the origin of Lyrical Ballads and 'that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith.'

Primary imagination: 'the living power and prime agent of all human perception ... a repetition in the finite mind of the eternal act of creation in the infinite I AM'; secondary imagination 'dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to re-create'; fancy deals with 'fixities and definites'.
Coleridge coined 'esemplastic' (shaping into one) for imagination; imagination 'reveals itself in the balance or reconciliation of opposite or discordant qualities'.
Chapters XVII-XXII of Biographia criticise Wordsworth's theory of poetic language; Table Talk (1827): prose = 'words in their best order', poetry = 'the best words in the best order'.
Coleridge's Shakespeare lectures distinguish organic form (grows from within) from mechanic form (imposed from outside), drawing on A.W. Schlegel.

topics.title: P. B. Shelley, Matthew Arnold and Walter Pater
points: Shelley's A Defence of Poetry, written 1821, published posthumously 1840, a reply to Thomas Love Peacock's The Four Ages of Poetry (1820).

Shelley quotes: 'Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world'; poetry is 'the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds'; 'the mind in creation is as a fading coal'; 'Reason is to imagination as the instrument to the agent.'

Arnold, 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time' (1864; Essays in Criticism, First Series, 1865): criticism is 'a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world'.

Arnold, 'The Study of Poetry' (1880, introduction to T.H. Ward's The English Poets; reprinted in Essays in Criticism, Second Series, 1888): poetry is 'a criticism of life'; he rejects the historical and personal estimates in favour of the real estimate.

Touchstone method: short lines from Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Milton used to test poetry; Chaucer lacks 'high seriousness' (Aristotle's spoudaiotes); Dryden and Pope are 'classics of our prose'; Burns also lacks high seriousness.
Arnold's Culture and Anarchy (1869): culture as 'sweetness and light', Hebraism vs Hellenism, classes as Barbarians, Philistines and Populace; he called Shelley 'a beautiful and ineffectual angel'.
Walter Pater, Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873); Conclusion: 'To burn always with this hard, gem-like flame, to maintain this ecstasy, is success in life.'
Pater, 'The School of Giorgione' (added 1877): 'All art constantly aspires towards the condition of music'; famous Mona Lisa passage: 'She is older than the rocks among which she sits.'

Pater's aesthetic/impressionistic criticism asks 'What is this song or picture ... to me?'; father of English Aestheticism ('art for art's sake'); other works Marius the Epicurean (1885), Appreciations (1889, with the essay 'Style').

topics.title: T. S. Eliot as Critic
points: 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919, The Egoist; collected in The Sacred Wood, 1920): tradition requires the 'historical sense' of 'not only the pastness of the past, but of its presence'.
Eliot's impersonal theory: 'Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion; it is not the expression of personality, but an escape from personality.'
Catalyst analogy: the poet's mind is like a filament of platinum which, introduced into oxygen and sulphur dioxide, forms sulphurous acid while itself remaining unchanged.
'The progress of an artist is a continual self-sacrifice, a continual extinction of personality'; 'Honest criticism and sensitive appreciation is directed not upon the poet but upon the poetry.'
'Hamlet and His Problems' (1919): coins/popularises the 'objective correlative'; calls Hamlet 'most certainly an artistic failure' and 'the Mona Lisa of literature'.

'The Metaphysical Poets' (1921, review of Grierson's anthology): 'dissociation of sensibility' set in during the 17th century, after Donne and the metaphysicals; for Donne 'a thought ... was an experience; it modified his sensibility.'

Other critical works: 'The Function of Criticism' (1923), Selected Essays (1932), The Use of Poetry and the Use of Criticism (1933, includes 'auditory imagination'), After Strange Gods (1934), Notes Towards the Definition of Culture (1948), 'The Frontiers of Criticism' (1956).
Eliot's essays helped revalue the metaphysical poets and Jacobean dramatists and dislodge Milton; he deeply influenced Leavis and the New Critics.
Eliot called himself 'classicist in literature, royalist in politics, and Anglo-Catholic in religion' (preface to For Lancelot Andrewes, 1928).

topics.title: I. A. Richards and William Empson
points: I.A. Richards (1893-1979), Cambridge: The Meaning of Meaning (1923, with C.K. Ogden), Principles of Literary Criticism (1924), Science and Poetry (1926), Practical Criticism (1929), The Philosophy of Rhetoric (1936).
Principles opens: 'A book is a machine to think with'; poetry's value lies in organising and balancing impulses (synaesthesis); poetry of inclusion vs poetry of exclusion.
Two uses of language: scientific/referential and emotive; poetic statements are 'pseudo-statements' which are not true or false like science.
Practical Criticism (1929): based on 'protocols' written by Cambridge students on 13 unsigned poems; lists reading difficulties like stock responses, sentimentality, doctrinal adhesions.
Four kinds of meaning in Practical Criticism: sense, feeling, tone and intention.
The Philosophy of Rhetoric (1936) introduces 'tenor' and 'vehicle' as the two parts of a metaphor.
William Empson (1906-1984), Richards's student at Cambridge: Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930), Some Versions of Pastoral (1935), The Structure of Complex Words (1951), Milton's God (1961).

Empson defines ambiguity as 'any verbal nuance, however slight, which gives room for alternative reactions to the same piece of language'; the first type is metaphor, the seventh is full contradiction showing a division in the author's mind.
Richards and Empson laid the ground for close reading and American New Criticism.

topics.title: F. R. Leavis
points: F.R. Leavis (1895-1978), Cambridge (Downing College); with wife Q.D. Leavis founded and edited Scrutiny (1932-1953).
Mass Civilization and Minority Culture (1930); Culture and Environment (1933, with Denys Thompson); Q.D. Leavis wrote Fiction and the Reading Public (1932).
New Bearings in English Poetry (1932): praises Eliot, Pound and Hopkins as the new direction of poetry.
Revaluation: Tradition and Development in English Poetry (1936): traces a line of wit from Donne; dislodges Milton.

The Great Tradition (1948) opens: 'The great English novelists are Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James and Joseph Conrad'; D.H. Lawrence added as heir; Dickens's Hard Times treated as a 'moral fable'.

Other works: The Common Pursuit (1952; title from Eliot's phrase 'the common pursuit of true judgment'), D.H. Lawrence: Novelist (1955), Two Cultures? The Significance of C.P. Snow (1962), The Living Principle (1975).
Key values: moral seriousness, 'life', concreteness, 'felt life', 'reverent openness before life'; literature as the centre of humane education.
Leavis's debate with René Wellek (1937) on whether a critic must state his philosophical norms; Leavis refused, insisting on 'Yes, but...' collaborative judgement.

topics.title: New Criticism: Ransom, Brooks, Tate, Wimsatt and Beardsley
points: American movement of the 1930s-50s, with roots in the Fugitives/Agrarians at Vanderbilt University; the name comes from John Crowe Ransom's book The New Criticism (1941).
Ransom: The World's Body (1938), essay 'Criticism, Inc.' (1937) calling for professional, objective criticism; poem has a logical 'structure' and local 'texture'; founded The Kenyon Review (1939).

Cleanth Brooks: Modern Poetry and the Tradition (1939); The Well Wrought Urn (1947) - essays 'The Language of Paradox' ('the language of poetry is the language of paradox') and 'The Heresy of Paraphrase'.
Brooks and Robert Penn Warren: Understanding Poetry (1938) and Understanding Fiction (1943), textbooks that spread close reading; they edited The Southern Review (1935).
Allen Tate, 'Tension in Poetry' (1938): good poetry has tension, formed by cutting the prefixes from 'extension' (denotation) and 'intension' (connotation).

W.K. Wimsatt and Monroe C. Beardsley, 'The Intentional Fallacy' (1946): 'the design or intention of the author is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging the success of a work of literary art.'
Wimsatt and Beardsley, 'The Affective Fallacy' (1949): confusing the poem with its results (what it does to the reader); both essays collected in Wimsatt's The Verbal Icon (1954).
Key tenets: the poem as an autonomous, organic 'verbal icon'; close reading of irony, paradox, ambiguity and tension; exclusion of biography, history and reader response.
Other New Critics: R.P. Blackmur, Yvor Winters, Robert Penn Warren; René Wellek and Austin Warren's Theory of Literature (1949) distinguishes 'intrinsic' and 'extrinsic' approaches.

topics.title: Northrop Frye: Archetypal Criticism
points: Canadian critic Northrop Frye (1912-1991): Fearful Symmetry (1947, on Blake), Anatomy of Criticism (1957), The Educated Imagination (1963), The Great Code: The Bible and Literature (1982).

Anatomy of Criticism has a 'Polemical Introduction' and four essays: Historical Criticism - Theory of Modes; Ethical Criticism - Theory of Symbols; Archetypal Criticism - Theory of Myths; Rhetorical Criticism - Theory of Genres.
Five fictional modes based on the hero's power of action: myth, romance, high mimetic, low mimetic and ironic.
Four mythoi linked with seasons: comedy - spring, romance - summer, tragedy - autumn, irony and satire - winter.
Four genres by 'radical of presentation': drama (acted), epos (recited), fiction/prose (read), lyric (overheard/sung).
Five phases of symbols: literal, descriptive, formal, mythical (archetypal) and anagogic.
Archetype: a typical or recurring image that connects one poem with another; 'displacement' adapts myth towards plausibility.
Frye wanted criticism to be a systematic 'science' and rejected 'value judgements' as part of the history of taste; drew on Jung and Frazer's The Golden Bough.

topics.title: Russian Formalism
points: Two groups: the Moscow Linguistic Circle (1915, led by Roman Jakobson) and OPOJAZ - Society for the Study of Poetic Language (Petrograd, 1916: Viktor Shklovsky, Boris Eichenbaum, Yury Tynyanov).

Viktor Shklovsky, 'Art as Technique' / 'Art as Device' (1917): art exists 'to make the stone stony'; ostranenie (defamiliarization, making strange) counters automatization; example from Tolstoy's 'Kholstomer' (story told by a horse).
Shklovsky: art is 'a way of experiencing the artfulness of an object; the object is not important'; Tristram Shandy called 'the most typical novel in world literature'.
Fabula (raw chronological story) vs syuzhet (plot as artistically arranged) - distinction developed by Shklovsky and Tomashevsky; Tomashevsky also distinguished bound and free motifs.
Jakobson coined 'literariness' (literaturnost, 1921): the object of literary science is not literature but what makes a given work literary.

Jakobson's 'Linguistics and Poetics' (1960): six factors and functions of communication; the poetic function 'projects the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection into the axis of combination'.
Tynyanov's 'On Literary Evolution' (1927) and the concept of the 'dominant'; Eichenbaum's 'The Theory of the Formal Method' (1926).
Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928): 31 functions and 7 spheres of action in Russian fairy tales; foundation of narratology.

Suppressed under Stalin around 1930; ideas continued in the Prague Linguistic Circle (1926; Jan Mukarovsky's 'foregrounding'); Bakhtin/Medvedev criticised it in The Formal Method in Literary Scholarship (1928); Victor Erlich's Russian Formalism: History-Doctrine (1955) introduced it to the West.

terms.hindi: नकल या अनुकरण; कला द्वारा दुनिया की नकल।
terms.net: Imitation or representation of reality in art; for Plato a copy of a copy 'thrice removed from truth', for Aristotle the natural basis of all poetry (Poetics).

terms.hindi: दर्शक के मन से करुणा और भय का शुद्धिकरण/विरेचन।
terms.net: Aristotle's term in the definition of tragedy (Poetics, Ch. 6) for the purgation or purification of pity and fear aroused in the audience.

terms.hindi: नायक की गलती या निर्णय की भूल जिससे उसका पतन होता है।
terms.net: Aristotle's 'error of judgement' or tragic flaw by which a hero of high fortune falls into misery (Poetics, Ch. 13).

terms.hindi: भाग्य का अचानक उलट जाना।
terms.net: Reversal of the situation: a change by which the action veers round to its opposite (Aristotle, Poetics Ch. 11), as when the messenger's news in Oedipus Rex produces the opposite effect.

terms.hindi: सच्चाई की पहचान या आत्म-बोध का क्षण।
terms.net: Recognition or discovery: 'a change from ignorance to knowledge' (Aristotle, Poetics Ch. 11), best when it coincides with peripeteia.

terms.hindi: नाटक में एक कथा, एक दिन और एक स्थान का नियम।
terms.net: Neoclassical rules of action, time and place; Aristotle stressed only unity of action, the unity of place being added by Castelvetro (1570).

terms.hindi: औचित्य; विषय और पात्र के अनुरूप भाषा-शैली।
terms.net: Propriety or fitness of style, diction and action to the character, subject and genre; a central principle of Horace's Ars Poetica and neoclassical criticism.

terms.hindi: कहानी को बीच से शुरू करना।
terms.net: Latin 'into the middle of things'; Horace's advice (Ars Poetica) that an epic should begin in the middle of the action, as Homer does.

terms.hindi: मनोरंजन और उपदेश दोनों।
terms.net: Horace's formula that poetry should be both sweet (pleasing) and useful (instructive); echoed by Sidney's 'to teach and delight'.

terms.hindi: उदात्त; ऐसी भव्यता जो मन को ऊपर उठा दे।
terms.net: Loftiness of thought and expression that produces transport (ekstasis) rather than persuasion; from Longinus's Peri Hupsous, 'the echo of a great soul'.

terms.hindi: काव्य या नाटक से मिलने वाला भावात्मक आनंद/रस।
terms.net: The aesthetic relish or emotional flavour evoked in the spectator, produced by the union of vibhava, anubhava and vyabhicharibhava (Bharata, Natyashastra).

terms.hindi: मन का स्थायी भाव, जैसे प्रेम, शोक, क्रोध।
terms.net: The permanent or dominant emotion latent in every person (rati, hasa, shoka etc.) which, when developed by vibhava and other bhavas, becomes rasa.

terms.hindi: भाव जगाने वाला कारण, जैसे पात्र या चाँदनी रात।
terms.net: Determinant or cause of emotion; divided into alambana (the object or person) and uddipana (the stimulating circumstances).

terms.hindi: भाव के बाहरी लक्षण, जैसे आँसू, मुस्कान।
terms.net: Consequent: the outward physical expression of an emotion, such as tears, glances or gestures, in Bharata's rasa sutra.

terms.hindi: क्षणिक या संचारी भाव जो आते-जाते रहते हैं।
terms.net: Transitory or fleeting emotional states (also sancharibhava) that strengthen the sthayibhava; Bharata lists 33 of them.

terms.hindi: समान हृदय वाला रसिक पाठक/दर्शक।
terms.net: The sensitive, cultivated reader or spectator 'of similar heart' who can relish rasa; a key idea of Anandavardhana and Abhinavagupta.

terms.hindi: भावों का सामान्य या सार्वभौमिक बन जाना।
terms.net: Generalisation or universalisation of emotions, freed from personal ties, so that the spectator enjoys rasa; theory of Bhatta Nayaka, developed by Abhinavagupta.

terms.hindi: व्यंजना; शब्दों से निकलने वाला छिपा अर्थ।
terms.net: Suggestion: the implied meaning conveyed through vyanjana beyond literal and secondary sense; declared the soul of poetry by Anandavardhana in Dhvanyaloka.

terms.hindi: शब्द का सीधा, शब्दकोश वाला अर्थ।
terms.net: Denotation: the primary power of a word to convey its literal, conventional meaning.

terms.hindi: लक्षणा; सीधा अर्थ न बैठने पर दूसरा अर्थ लेना।
terms.net: Indication or secondary meaning used when the literal sense is blocked, e.g. 'a village on the Ganga' meaning on its bank.

terms.hindi: शब्द की वह शक्ति जो संकेत से अर्थ देती है।
terms.net: Suggestive power of words, beyond abhidha and lakshana, through which dhvani and rasa are conveyed.

terms.hindi: ऐसा काव्य जिसमें छिपा अर्थ गौण हो।
terms.net: Anandavardhana's 'middle' poetry, in which the suggested meaning is subordinate to the expressed meaning.

terms.hindi: काव्य का आभूषण; उपमा, रूपक आदि।
terms.net: Figure of speech or poetic ornament (shabdalankara and arthalankara); the Alankara school of Bhamaha and Dandin made it the essence of poetry.

terms.hindi: काव्य की शैली या शब्द-रचना का ढंग।
terms.net: Style, defined by Vamana as 'vishishta padarachana' (special arrangement of words) and declared the soul of poetry; three kinds: Vaidarbhi, Gaudi, Panchali.

terms.hindi: टेढ़ी या चमत्कारपूर्ण उक्ति।
terms.net: Oblique, striking or deviant expression; Kuntaka in Vakroktijivita called it the life of poetry and analysed six levels of vakrata.

terms.hindi: उचितता; हर चीज़ का सही जगह, सही ढंग से होना।
terms.net: Propriety or appropriateness; Kshemendra in Auchitya-vichara-charcha called it the abiding life of poetry full of rasa.

terms.hindi: कविता के लिए बनावटी, बोलचाल से अलग भाषा।
terms.net: Language and phrasing held proper to poetry and distinct from ordinary speech, typical of 18th-century verse; attacked by Wordsworth in the Preface to Lyrical Ballads.

terms.hindi: कल्पना का निचला, यांत्रिक रूप जो चीज़ों को जोड़ता भर है।
terms.net: Coleridge's term (Biographia Literaria, Ch. XIII) for the associative faculty that plays with 'fixities and definites', inferior to imagination.

terms.hindi: अनेक चीज़ों को एक रूप में ढालने वाली।
terms.net: Word coined by Coleridge (Biographia Literaria) for the unifying, shaping power of the imagination, 'to shape into one'.

terms.hindi: कहानी को सच मानने के लिए अविश्वास को कुछ देर छोड़ देना।
terms.net: Coleridge's phrase (Biographia Literaria, Ch. XIV): 'that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith.'

terms.hindi: कसौटी; अच्छी कविता परखने का पैमाना।
terms.net: Arnold's method in 'The Study of Poetry' (1880) of judging poetry by comparing it with short passages from the great masters such as Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Milton.

terms.hindi: गहरी गंभीरता जो महान कविता में होती है।
terms.net: Arnold's quality of great poetry, after Aristotle's spoudaiotes; he denied it to Chaucer and Burns in 'The Study of Poetry'.

terms.hindi: कला केवल कला के लिए, नैतिक उपदेश के लिए नहीं।
terms.net: Late-19th-century doctrine of 'art for art's sake', associated in England with Walter Pater and Oscar Wilde, valuing beauty and intense experience above morality.

terms.hindi: भावना जगाने वाली ठोस घटनाएँ या वस्तुएँ।
terms.net: Eliot's term ('Hamlet and His Problems', 1919): 'a set of objects, a situation, a chain of events which shall be the formula of that particular emotion.'

terms.hindi: विचार और भावना का अलग-अलग हो जाना।
terms.net: Eliot's phrase ('The Metaphysical Poets', 1921) for the split between thought and feeling that set in in English poetry in the 17th century, after the metaphysicals.

terms.hindi: कवि का अपने निजी भावों से दूर रहना।
terms.net: Eliot's doctrine ('Tradition and the Individual Talent', 1919) that poetry is 'an escape from personality', the poet's mind being like a catalyst.

terms.hindi: ऐसा कथन जो सच-झूठ नहीं, भावना के लिए होता है।
terms.net: I.A. Richards's term (Science and Poetry, 1926) for poetic statements valued for their emotional effect, not for scientific truth.

terms.hindi: रूपक का मूल विषय और जिस चीज़ से तुलना की जाती है।
terms.net: Richards's terms (The Philosophy of Rhetoric, 1936) for the subject of a metaphor (tenor) and the image that carries it (vehicle).

terms.hindi: एक ही शब्द/पंक्ति के कई अर्थ होना।
terms.net: Empson's 'any verbal nuance, however slight, which gives room for alternative reactions to the same piece of language' (Seven Types of Ambiguity, 1930).

terms.hindi: पाठ के हर शब्द को ध्यान से पढ़कर अर्थ निकालना।
terms.net: Detailed analysis of the words, images and structure of a text in isolation from biography and history; method of Richards, Empson and the New Critics.

terms.hindi: लेखक के इरादे से रचना को परखने की भूल।
terms.net: Wimsatt and Beardsley (1946): the error of judging a work by the author's intention, which is 'neither available nor desirable' as a standard.

terms.hindi: पाठक पर प्रभाव से रचना को परखने की भूल।
terms.net: Wimsatt and Beardsley (1949): 'a confusion between the poem and its results', judging it by its emotional effect on the reader.

terms.hindi: कविता का सार अपने शब्दों में कहकर उसे समझ लेने की भूल।
terms.net: Cleanth Brooks's term (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947) for the mistaken belief that a poem's meaning can be reduced to a prose statement.

terms.hindi: विरोधाभास; ऊपर से उल्टा लगने वाला पर सच्चा कथन।
terms.net: An apparently self-contradictory statement that reveals a truth; for Brooks 'the language of poetry is the language of paradox'.

terms.hindi: कविता में शाब्दिक और भावार्थ के बीच का संतुलित खिंचाव।
terms.net: Allen Tate's term ('Tension in Poetry', 1938) made by removing the prefixes of extension and intension: the organised whole of a poem's meanings.

terms.hindi: बार-बार आने वाला मूल प्रतीक या कथा-ढाँचा।
terms.net: A recurring image, symbol, character type or plot pattern; for Frye 'a typical or recurring image' connecting one poem with another (Anatomy of Criticism, 1957).

terms.hindi: जानी-पहचानी चीज़ को नया और अजनबी बनाकर दिखाना।
terms.net: Ostranenie, 'making strange': Shklovsky's term ('Art as Technique', 1917) for art's power to renew perception dulled by habit, 'to make the stone stony'.

terms.hindi: घटनाओं का असली क्रम और कथा में उनकी प्रस्तुति।
terms.net: Russian Formalist distinction between the chronological sequence of events (fabula, story) and their artistic arrangement in the narrative (syuzhet, plot).

terms.hindi: वह गुण जो किसी रचना को साहित्य बनाता है।
terms.net: Literaturnost, Jakobson's term (1921) for the specific features that make a text literary, the true object of literary study.

terms.hindi: भाषा के किसी हिस्से को उभारकर ध्यान खींचना।
terms.net: Aktualisace, Jan Mukarovsky's (Prague School) term for bringing language to the reader's attention by deviation from norms of ordinary speech.

mcqs.q: Who said that art is 'thrice removed from the truth'?
mcqs.exp: Plato in Republic Book X calls the imitative artist a copier of appearances, thrice removed from the Idea.

mcqs.q: In which dialogue does Plato compare poetic inspiration to a magnet attracting iron rings?
mcqs.exp: The magnet image of Muse-poet-rhapsode-audience appears in Ion.

mcqs.q: Arrange Aristotle's six parts of tragedy in his order of importance: (a) Character (b) Spectacle (c) Plot (d) Diction
mcqs.exp: Plot, Character, Thought, Diction, Song, Spectacle.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Aristotle considers poetry more philosophical than history. Reason (R): Poetry expresses the universal, history the particular.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Poetics Ch. 9 gives exactly this reason.

mcqs.q: Which unity was NOT insisted upon by Aristotle but added later by Castelvetro?
mcqs.exp: Aristotle stressed unity of action and mentioned a single revolution of the sun; Castelvetro (1570) added place.

mcqs.q: 'Even good Homer nods' and 'purple patches' come from:
mcqs.exp: Both phrases are from Horace's Ars Poetica.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Longinus's five sources of the sublime?
mcqs.exp: Longinus's sources: thought, passion, figures, diction, elevated composition.

mcqs.q: 'Sublimity is the echo of a great soul' was said by:
mcqs.exp: From Longinus's Peri Hupsous.

mcqs.q: Match the List I with List II: (a) Dhvanyaloka (b) Vakroktijivita (c) Kavyalankarasutravritti (d) Auchitya-vichara-charcha | (i) Kuntaka (ii) Vamana (iii) Kshemendra (iv) Anandavardhana
mcqs.exp: Anandavardhana-Dhvanyaloka, Kuntaka-Vakroktijivita, Vamana-Riti text, Kshemendra-Auchitya.

mcqs.q: According to Bharata's rasa sutra, rasa arises from the union of:
mcqs.exp: 'Vibhavanubhava-vyabhichari-samyogad rasa-nishpattih'.

mcqs.q: Which rasa was not among Bharata's original eight and was firmly established by Abhinavagupta?
mcqs.exp: Shanta is the ninth rasa defended by Abhinavagupta.

mcqs.q: Match the sthayibhava with its rasa: (a) Jugupsa (b) Utsaha (c) Vismaya (d) Shoka | (i) Karuna (ii) Adbhuta (iii) Vira (iv) Bibhatsa
mcqs.exp: Jugupsa-Bibhatsa, Utsaha-Vira, Vismaya-Adbhuta, Shoka-Karuna.

mcqs.q: Abhinavagupta's interpretation of the rasa sutra is known as:
mcqs.exp: Lollata-utpatti, Shankuka-anumiti, Bhatta Nayaka-bhukti, Abhinavagupta-abhivyakti.

mcqs.q: According to Anandavardhana, poetry in which the suggested meaning is subordinate to the expressed meaning is called:
mcqs.exp: Gunibhuta vyangya is the middle grade of poetry.

mcqs.q: Who declared 'ritir atma kavyasya' (riti is the soul of poetry)?
mcqs.exp: Vamana founded the Riti school.

mcqs.q: Identify the correct chronological sequence: (a) Anandavardhana (b) Bharata (c) Kshemendra (d) Bhamaha
mcqs.exp: Bharata, Bhamaha (6th-7th c.), Anandavardhana (9th c.), Kshemendra (11th c.).

mcqs.q: Sidney's An Apology for Poetry was a reply to:
options: Peacock's The Four Ages of Poetry
Puttenham's The Art of English Poesy
Rymer's A Short View of Tragedy
mcqs.exp: Stephen Gosson's 1579 attack was dedicated to Sidney.

mcqs.q: Who wrote, 'the poet, he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth'?
mcqs.exp: Sidney, An Apology for Poetry.

mcqs.q: In Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy, which speaker represents Dryden himself?
mcqs.exp: Neander ('new man') is Dryden and defends English drama.

mcqs.q: Who called Dryden 'the father of English criticism'?
mcqs.exp: Johnson in the Life of Dryden.

mcqs.q: 'True wit is Nature to advantage dressed, / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed' is from:
mcqs.exp: Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711).

mcqs.q: Who described metaphysical poetry as one in which 'the most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together'?
mcqs.exp: Johnson, Life of Cowley in Lives of the Poets.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Johnson defends Shakespeare's mingling of tragic and comic scenes. Reason (R): Such drama exhibits the real state of sublunary nature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare (1765) gives this very reason.

mcqs.q: In which chapter of Biographia Literaria does Coleridge distinguish primary imagination, secondary imagination and fancy?
mcqs.exp: Chapter XIII; Chapter XIV has 'willing suspension of disbelief'.

mcqs.q: 'Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world' occurs in a work written in reply to:
mcqs.exp: Shelley's A Defence of Poetry answered Peacock's The Four Ages of Poetry.

mcqs.q: Which poet does Arnold say lacks 'high seriousness' in 'The Study of Poetry'?
mcqs.exp: Arnold praises Chaucer's liquid diction but denies him high seriousness.

mcqs.q: 'All art constantly aspires towards the condition of music' is a statement by:
mcqs.exp: Pater, 'The School of Giorgione', in The Renaissance.

mcqs.q: Match the List I with List II: (a) Objective correlative (b) Pseudo-statement (c) Intentional fallacy (d) Defamiliarization | (i) Shklovsky (ii) Wimsatt and Beardsley (iii) I.A. Richards (iv) T.S. Eliot
mcqs.exp: Eliot, Richards, Wimsatt-Beardsley and Shklovsky respectively.

mcqs.q: Which four novelists form F.R. Leavis's 'great tradition' in the opening of The Great Tradition (1948)?
options: Austen, George Eliot, Henry James, Conrad
mcqs.exp: Leavis's opening sentence names Austen, George Eliot, James and Conrad.

mcqs.q: In Frye's Anatomy of Criticism, which mythos is associated with autumn?
mcqs.exp: Comedy-spring, romance-summer, tragedy-autumn, irony/satire-winter.
